purpose: Separate food-price indexes and dollar sales from the physical/unit quantity of food purchased when evaluating affordability and downstream transmission claims.
scope: United States retail food and beverage, February-April 2026

observations.interpretation: Consumers spent more dollars while purchasing fewer units year over year.
Dollar sales rose while unit volume was essentially flat year over year.
Physical/unit demand fell substantially faster than dollar sales. Calendar effects, including Easter timing, remain a material confounder.

price_index_context.rule: The monthly CPI movement measures an average price-index change, not household affordability and not physical food quantity purchased.

interpretive_rules: Dollar sales, price indexes, units purchased, weight/volume, package size, household basket quality, and purchasing power are distinct state variables.
Unit sales are a closer proxy for physical purchasing than dollar sales but are not identical to pounds, kilograms, calories, or nutritional quantity because package sizes and product mix differ.
A decline in CPI cannot be interpreted as increased food consumption volume without quantity evidence.
Dollar growth accompanied by flat or falling units is evidence consistent with consumers paying more per unit/mix while not receiving proportionally more physical food.
Department-level divergence must remain visible; aggregate food volume can mask substitution across categories.
No household-level or state-level conclusion is authorized from national aggregate scanner data alone.
bounded_finding: The February-March national retail evidence is more consistent with constrained food purchasing than with improved grocery affordability: February food/beverage units fell despite higher dollar sales, and March unit sales were essentially flat while dollar sales rose. April unit sales then fell sharply, though calendar effects complicate the comparison.
